Error: cannot allocate vector of size 1.4 Gb
 I tried with 32GB RAM  with 32 Core system The error is the same cannot allocate vector of size only the memory size differs. The models are listed below
m1 <- openCR.fit(CH,mask=msk, type = 'CJSsecr',model = list(lambda~t, phi~t))
m.s<- openCR.fit(CH,mask=msk, type = 'CJSsecr',model = list(lambda~t, phi~sex))
Could you have any solution to deal this?

regards:
Ujjwal

messages.subject: Re: Problem in running OpenCR
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ujjwal
You imply that the model fits and then falls over - that is odd. lambda is not a parameter in the CJSsecr model, and maybe the problem has something to do with that. Otherwise, I think you're going to have to trouble shoot this yourself by trying simpler models or compacting the data.
- try non-spatial models first
- try constant models first
- check the size of your habitat mask (around 1000 points should be enough for a start)
- do not use daily 'occasions' within each year

Note also that CJSsecr is unsafe, and ultimately you will want to use JSSAsecrf or similar.
Murray

messages.subject: Re: Questions about sex-specific estimates
messages.body_plain:
Good day,
We're trying to estimate sex-specific and total black bear densities from hair snag data from multiple independent trap arrays. We'd also like to be able to estimate average density across several arrays, with standard errors and asymmetrical (back-transformed) confidence limits. However, I'm having difficulty extracting or calculating the standard error of total bear density on the link scale from the individual trap arrays.

We have already fit sets of candidate models to each data set using the conditional likelihood with sex as a covariate, and estimated density from AICc-minimizing models. We can easily calculate total and sex-specific densities, with SEs and CIs on the "real" (response) scale, using derived(). I can also use the delta method to calculate average variances and SEs of total density across across multiple traplines, but since these are on the real scale associated confidence limits are symmetrical around the average density.  I don't know how to calculate or extract an SE for density on the link scale from the output from derived().

I found this thread and modeled sexes as sessions in a full likelihood model to see if I could use the contrasts method Murray provided an example of.  I used the detection model from the AICc-minimizing CL model and tried both D~sex (as sessions) and D~1. The model with sex-specific density yielded the same density estimates as the CL model; the model with constant density yielded a slightly lower estimate.  When I tried to apply the contrast method to the model with sex-specific density, it reports density as half the total density from the model with constant density.  The model with sex-specific density was supported by AICc, and we expect higher female than male density.  Also there is still no SE on the link scale, so I still wouldn't be able to use the delta method to calculate average D across traplines. The contrasts method therefore doesn't seem useful in this particular case(??).

I also calculated total density (both sexes) and used the delta method to obtain the SE and CIs for total density from the fitted FL model with sex-specific density, as follows:

fit.LR=secr.fit(Dat.LR, model= list(D~session,g0~1,sigma~T+session), mask=mask.LR, details=list(contrasts=list(session=contr.sum)))
reals =predict(fit.LR,realnames='D',type="response")
total.D=log(reals[[1]][1,2]+reals[[2]][1,2]) # yields total D on link scale; backtransforming gives same estimate as derived(CL model).
#
delta.mo = function(se) {
  vr=se^2
  mean.vr=sum(vr) / length(vr)
  mean.se=sqrt(mean.vr)
  return(mean.se)
}
#
betas=predict(fit.LR, realnames='D', type="link")
mean.se = delta.mo(se=c(betas[[1]][1,3],betas[[2]][1,3]))
CI = c(mean.d - (1.96*mean.se), mean.d + (1.96*mean.se))
#
real.D.CI = c(exp(mean.d), exp(CI))
real.D.CI
# 0.0015536801  0.0006751119  0.0035755877

The resulting density estimate matches the one obtained using derived(CL model) (below), but my delta method confidence intervals are quite a bit wider.
D = 0.001553678, SE = 0.0005069814, CI = 0.0008329 - 0.00289816.

So, my approach would provide the SE around total density on the link scale needed to calculate SEs and asymmetrical confidence limits around average D across traplines, but seems to sacrifice precision.

We know that we could fit models to multisession data with sex as a covariate and trap arrays as sessions to obtain average density across the arrays. I've haven't done so (yet) because detection models with slightly different forms were supported for the different data sets. This is probably simply because the true model is not (ever) in the candidate set, and similar but not identical models were supported due to sampling variation between the traplines. However, perhaps bear behaviour actually differed among arrays, in which case we'd need a detection model with a lot of interactions with session to model detection appropriately. This seems less than ideal. We will likely try fitting multisession models with with the most commonly-supported forms of variation in detection parameters, and additive session effects (if supported), to pooled data, but I'd still like to find a solution to the problem described above if possible.

I think what would be best for us is if we could calculate or extract the SE around total density on the link scale from the CL models. Is this possible?  Then we could estimate density from the AICc-supported detection model for each trapline, and calculate average density across traplines (all used the same # of traps and covered a similar area) and SEs and asymmetrical CIs using the delta method (right?).

messages.body_plain:
Hi Eric
I have yet to digest your whole post, but starting at the bottom...
- variances for derived D are inherently slightly ad hoc, as they use my application of the Huggins non-spatial variance that no statistician has spent time on (see the 'supplements' to our 2008 paper that I wrote, not David).
- have you noticed that the default (loginterval = TRUE) is for derived() to compute CL on the log (i.e. default link) scale? The code for this is buried in an internal function (called by derived.secr, see getAnywhere(derived.secr)) that you can access with secr:::add.cl <http://add.cl>. This uses a (delta method) estimate of the log-scale SE. You could easily adapt this.
- in case it's relevant and you forgot, there is the opportunity to define groups post-hoc in derived.secr (groups argument).
Murray

Thanks very much Murray,

I looked at the code for derived() and add.cl <http://add.cl>(),
It seems that obtaining the SE, on the (log) link scale, around the density estimated by applying derived() to an secr model object created by fitting the conditional likelihood is as simple as:

# where "der" is the data frame created when one applies derived() to a fitted model,
# such that der[2,1] and der[2,2] are the estimated density and it's SE on the real scale, respectively:
#
SE.derived.D= function(der) {
  se.D.link = sqrt(log(1+(der[2,2] / der[2,1])^2))
  return(se.D.link)
}

I used the SE I obtained to manually calculate confidence limits on the link scale and then back-transformed them to the real scale. The results matched those from derived().

I also compared the result obtained using the above to the beta coefficients obtained by fitting a full likelihood model (same detection model, sexes modeled as sessions) to the same data.
The CL model, derived, and the above function yielded an SE on the link scale of 0.1625689 (this is around the total density of both sexes, but density differs between sexes because the detection model included sex effects on g0 and sigma).
The FL model yielded SE.beta of 0.16144109 around the first density parameter (intercept), and 0.16135984 around the second density parameter (effect of session, i.e. of sex).

This should serve our purposes well.

Thanks again,
Eric Howe

Hello

Foreword: I am reposting so Murray and I can continue this conversation here where it can be documented/used by others. So far he has suggested that I shouldn’t run a model where Lamba0 varies by trap_type without doing the same for sigma. This confuses me a bit, as I don’t expect the spatial scale of the detections to differ between the traps, I just know that one of the two trap types has ~1/4 the detection probability. Does that make sense or am I missing something? Murray also asked why I am using ~b, when I say ~bk usually fit well in our density models, which I only did because I didn’t see a bk option, only b, based on table 5 from the vignette (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/openCR/vignettes/openCR-vignette.pdf)

Two questions/observations as I work with the new openCR package:

1) I fit simple models for detection: ~1, ~b, ~ trap_type, ~trap_type+b. We know that our trap types (bait sites and rub trees) differ largely in their detection probability, and we often see the bk variable come out in density models, so these seemed like good candidate models. I found the results (screenshot attached) a bit confusing, as the trap_type variable drops out, and we know that this has a big effect on detection (Lamb et al. 2016 and work by others). I see that the trap variables add much information over the null, but somehow this b variable alone is better explaining the variation in detection than trap type. This seems odd to me. Do you have any insight?

2) My main goal is to estimate trend, and any variation in the trend through time. Just for illustrative purposes, I ran models that allowed for two values of population growth to be estimated, one in the early portion of the study (2006-2012) and one in the later (2012-2013). I ran these models with the ~ trap_type and ~trap_type+b detection variables . Surprisingly (which I say because I find density results from ‘secr’ to be rather insensitive to different detection covariates in my experience), the trend flips either increasing then decreasing, or decreasing then increasing, depending on the detection covariates used (results in screenshot, I use the derived density just to show the trends). This too seemed odd to me, and I found the sensitivity in the results concerning. Previously, we had shown a decline, using non-spatial open models between 2006-2013, so I am surprised to see a possible increase during this period with the inclusion of the b variable. Again, any thoughts on this?

Appreciate it,
Clayton

For trend estimation only, I wonder (leaving any answers for Murray) whether the benefits of an open model (I guess Markovian constraints on changes in N?) outweigh the benefits of tackling this from a multi-session/strata perspective (the ability to explicitly model changes in D as spatial, temporal effects).

I think I follow the logic when it applies to individual variation (or say, landscape variation and RSF betas vs. lam0/sigma)--moving further distances suggests spending less time at any one location--but as a source of trap/point variation, I'm confused. Detectable space is so small for a hair-catch, camera, etc. that it seems to me that there could plausibly be an effect on lam0 without compensation in sigma because for some of these detectors, detection might be more sensitive to factors other than broad-scale movement. For a rub tree, lam0 seems to be a product of the frequency of being next to the tree and the likelihood or frequency of choosing to rub. Some jaguar studies suggest that females use less space than males, but also don't use big trails where the researchers are placing cameras. Certainly, females have to be spending more time off-trail, but for the purposes of detection given the design, female sigma and lam0 might be smaller. I'm curious as to what I'm missing or misunderstanding.

For the record, my original offlist reply was

"Nothing much to say here - you are the one close to the data who can figure this out! It is inherently risky (and in my view illogical) to model lambda0 as a function of trap type while keeping sigma constant. Why if ~bk is a good model do you fit ~b?"

I stand by my statement about lambda0 and sigma, which was not directly about compensation. Detection probability is a function of both parameters (not lambda0 alone). Fixing sigma across types only makes sense if you are sure there no broad-sense behavioural effects. In Clayton's case it is entirely possible that the probability of interacting with a detector, given presence at the point, depends on where the detector is in the home range and differs between the two detector types; that would lead to a difference in sigma between types. Remember I was just throwing out cheap advice. Compensation is another story (both relevant and a perhaps red herring).

I had forgotten that openCR does not offer ~bk, but ~b is not a substitute - they are different models usually leading to quite different estimates (~bk often gives estimated densities close to null-model densities). There are also tricky questions about the duration of a learned response - I would skip it.

We have a lot to learn about the behaviour of open spatial models!

Murray

I can't remember why there is no bk model in openCR. For fun I generated one with the custom design data option (see vignette):

makedf.bk <- function (ch, nmix = 1) {
    ch <- squeeze(ch)
    # Construct array of logical values TRUE iff caught at k on or before s
    detected.at.k <- apply(abs(ch), c(1,3), cumsum) > 0
    # TRUE only if detected at k before occasion s
    bk <- apply(detected.at.k, 2:3, function(x) {x[which.max(x)] <- FALSE; x})
    bk <- aperm(bk, c(2,1,3))
    n <- nrow(ch)
    S <- ncol(ch)
    K <- dim(ch)[3]
    data.frame(bk = insertdim(bk, 1:3, c(n,S,K,nmix)))
}
